whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows glory lived out in chebar canal, babylon. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: “You, son of man, take a sharp sword. You shall take it as a barber’s razor to yourself, and shall cause it to pass over your head and over your beard. Then take balances to weigh and divide the hair.
I will do in you that which I have not done, and which I will not do anything like it any more, because of all your abominations.
I will send on you famine and evil animals, and they will bereave you. Pestilence and blood will pass through you. I will bring the sword on you. I, Yahweh, have spoken it.’”

questions.question: What is happening in Ezekiel 5?
questions.answer: In 17 verses, this chapter ezekiel 5 (17 verses) continues the story of glory. starting with '“you, son of man, take a sharp sword. you shall take it as a barber’s razor to yourself, and shall cause it to pass over your head and over your beard. then tak', it moves through themes of glory, idolatry and calls readers toward new heart. The setting is chebar canal, babylon, written to exiles in babylon. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote Ezekiel and why 5 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally ezekiel, addressed to exiles in babylon around ~593-571 bc. This chapter fits the book's purpose as visions, oracles — its themes of glory, idolatry build on what came before.

questions.question: Are there any difficult words here?
questions.answer: Scan for names, places, or repeated abstract words like righteousness, covenant, or glory. The glossary below defines up to 3 that show up most. Ask: who is this person, what does this word mean in everyday terms?

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through glory and idolatry, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 2 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: 'A third part you shall burn in the fire in the middle of the city, when the days of the siege are fulfilled. You shall take a third part, and strike with the sword around it. A thi...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about glory. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?
